title: US intel officials postpone classified threat briefing for election officials after technical difficulties | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

US intelligence officials had to postpone a much-anticipated classified briefing for election officials about foreign threats because the video call was plagued by technical difficulties, according to six people familiar with the matter.

Election officials from across the country, who rearranged their schedules on short notice less than three weeks before Election Day, were left frustrated after federal officials were unable to get the video call to work on Thursday, the sources said.

The briefing was set to be the first time since the 2024 presidential election that state election officials heard from federal agencies in a classified setting about the threat environment from foreign powers like Russia, Iran and China, according to three of the sources.

Officials from the FBI and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence planned to lead the briefing, while the Department of Homeland Security’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) was supposed to help facilitate it.

“Glad they don’t run the election,” one person familiar with the call said, referring to the federal officials who organized the call.

Invites to election officials went out just a couple days prior to the briefing, and some election officials who wanted to get access to the briefing were unable to, one of the sources familiar with the call said.

One county election director said their security team wasn’t able to connect to the briefing due to the technical difficulties. An election official in another state said the briefing was “abruptly cancelled” about 15 to 30 minutes after it was scheduled to begin, and that the federal officials didn’t offer much explanation.

CNN has requested comment from all three federal agencies that hosted the aborted briefing.

The mishap comes as many Americans have already cast their ballots in the midterm elections, and as US intelligence officials continue to monitor for attempts by foreign powers such as Russia and Iran to sow discord among voters.

At least one election official who spoke to CNN pointed out that the briefing was supposed to take place the same week that multiple election officesreceived suspicious letterscontaining white powders. That matter is now under investigation by the FBI, and the briefing Thursday was unrelated to the letters.

The blunders in organizing Thursday’s briefing stem from the fact that federal officials in the second Trump administration have not been in touch as regularly with election officials about security issues as in prior administrations, three of the sources said.

In the first Trump administration and the Biden administration after, the FBI, CISA and ODNI regularly briefed election officials on the latest intelligence on Russia, Iran and China’s possible intentions toward the midterm and general elections. The briefings covered hacking threats, disinformation and other activity emanating from those nations and from others.

But the second Trump administrationdisbanded or downsizedseveral government centers that were tasked with repelling foreign influence operations. The administration also dismantled CISA’s election security work and fired or reassigned many of the agency’s experts on the subject. In the last three months, the Trump administration has begun to rebuild some of that election security work while continuing to pursue evidence that supports the president’s false claims of widespread election fraud.

In June, CISA told Congress that it had assigned new officials to build “trusted relationships” with state and local elected officials, CNN hasreported.

Last month, Defense Secretary Pete Hegsethsigneda memo directing the military to defend the US midterm elections from foreign interference. The activities outlined in the memo are largely things that US military and spy agencies were doing to protect American elections from foreign threats prior to Donald Trump returning to the presidency in 2025.

Trump has also continued to dismiss orquestionpast US intelligence about Russian and Chinese efforts to influence elections. Those factors prompted widespread concern among current and former US national security officials that the second Trump administration was not prioritizing defending US elections from foreign meddling.
